abstract: Long-awaited results from phase III trial show huge benefits for treatment-resistant melanoma.

title: RES NPs/GelMA Sustained-Release Cryogel Modulates Macrophage Arachidonic Acid Metabolism and Angiogenic Microenvironment Promoting Diabetic Wound Healing
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Refractory chronic diabetic wounds severely impair quality of life. Their delayed healing is mainly driven by impaired angiogenesis and persistent inflammation caused by infection and excessive ROS. Resveratrol (RES) has anti-inflammatory and pro-angiogenic effects, but its clinical use is limited by poor solubility and low bioavailability. Here, we developed a dual-mechanism sustained-release system for RES to promote diabetic wound healing. RES was converted into nanoparticles (RES NPs) to improve cellular uptake and bioavailability, then encapsulated in GelMA cryogel microspheres (CMS) for injectable, sustained release. This system downregulated NF-κB signaling, reduced ROS, and suppressed pro-inflammatory cytokines and COX2, thereby inhibiting arachidonic acid metabolism and promoting macrophage polarization from M1 to M2. Meanwhile, AMPK activation restored endothelial cell function, enhanced angiogenesis, and supported new vessel formation. Overall, this strategy accelerated high-quality wound repair in diabetic conditions.

title: Reversing Electrochemical Spongification by Asymmetric Breathing for 380‐hour Hydroxylamine Electrosynthesis
abstract: ABSTRACT Electrocatalytic nitrate‐to‐hydroxylamine (NH 2 OH) conversion offers a sustainable route for reactive nitrogen upcycling. Metallic bismuth (Bi) is intrinsically active for this reaction, yet undergoes severe structural degradation under continuous electrolysis—a failure mode we identify as electrochemical spongification, wherein the compact Bi framework cathodically relaxes into an electrically disconnected porous network. Herein, we report an “asymmetric electrochemical breathing” strategy that effectively decouples long‐term catalytic durability from structural failure. Using pulsed potentials between −1.36 and +1.24 V versus the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE), BiOCl nanosheets serve as a dynamic template, delivering a high Faradaic efficiency of 71.7% and a yield rate of 4.29 mmol h −1 cm −2 , among the highest reported for NH 2 OH electrosynthesis. Experimental and theoretical insights reveal that BiOCl rapidly reduces in situ to dense metallic Bi to drive efficient nitrate reduction. Crucially, a brief anodic pulse reconstructs the framework before irreversible degradation occurs, enabling continuous structural rejuvenation for over 380 h. This dynamic reconstruction strategy successfully suppresses the Faradaic efficiency decay rate by two orders of magnitude, establishing a robust paradigm for stabilizing highly active yet metastable electrocatalysts.

title: Electrosynthesis of p ‐Hydroxybenzoic Acid From Phenol and CO 2
abstract: ABSTRACT P ‐hydroxybenzoic acid ( p ‐HBA), with wide applications in food preservatives, pesticides, pharmaceuticals, and liquid crystalline polyether, is currently synthesized via the Kolbe–Schmitt reaction using anhydrous phenolate (PhO − ) and carbon dioxide (CO 2 ). However, this reaction typically suffers from poor selectivity, and requires high temperature/pressure, strongly base, and metal/organic cations for selectivity control. Herein, we report a new method for the electrosynthesis of p ‐HBA from phenol (PhOH) and CO 2 by iodine mediation, achieving 61% yield and 90% selectivity without strong bases and metal cations under ambient temperature and pressure conditions. Mechanism studies indicated that PhOH was first selectively iodinated by iodine cations (I + ) generated at the anode to form p ‐iodophenol (HOPh‐I). Subsequently, HOPh‐I and CO 2 were respectively activated on Ag catalyst with abundant grain boundaries (GB‐Ag) through single‐electron reduction, and then underwent radical coupling processes to produce p ‐HBA. Notably, this electrochemical method also successfully converted various oxygen‐containing and nitrogen‐containing aromatic compounds, including the typical structural units of lignin and its derivatives, into valuable carboxylic acids. This innovative electrochemical approach overcomes the inherent limitations of the traditional Kolbe–Schmitt reaction, offering a promising strategy for the sustainable utilization of CO 2 and biomass resources.

title: Breaking the π‐Conjugation‐Dependence: Enhanced Birefringence and SHG Response in Densely Packed Deep‐UV Phosphates
abstract: ABSTRACT Optimizing birefringence and SHG in deep‐UV NLO crystals based on tetrahedral oxyanions remains challenging as extending π‐conjugation often sacrifices UV transparency. In this study, we propose a synergic design strategy that correlates π‐conjugation degree, packing density, and optical performance, resulting in two formamidinium phosphate crystals, enabling two deep‐UV NLO crystals, [CH(NH 2 ) 2 ]H 2 PO 4 ( I ) and [CH(NH 2 ) 2 ] 2 HPO 4 ( II ), with simultaneously enhanced birefringence (0.10@550 nm of I and 0.15@550 nm of II ) and SHG responses (1.1 × KDP of I and 2.0 × KDP of II ). Notably, birefringence of compound II outperforms a number of guanidinium‐based and phosphate‐based NLO crystals, endowing it with exceptional comprehensive performance, as evidenced by its highest quality factor ( Q = 4.4 for II) . Due to the superior birefringence and SHG intensity, both I and II realize phase‐matching at fundamental wavelength of 1064 nm and 532 nm. Structure–property relationship studies reveal that formamidinium's small steric size facilitates dense packing of building blocks within lattice, thereby enhancing birefringence and SHG. This work elucidates the critical influence of π‐conjugation degree on packing density and overall performance (SHG intensity and birefringence). Based on these findings, a novel design pathway for deep‐UV materials might be proposed, linking π‐conjugation degree and packing density with SHG and birefringence.

title: Ni 3 (HITP) 2 @PTFE Molecular Fence Enables Selective C 2 Coupling in Methane Contact‐Electro‐Catalysis
abstract: ABSTRACT Contact‐Electro‐Catalysis (CEC) enables methane activation under ambient conditions; however, the poorly understood interfacial active sites and uncontrolled evolution of reactive radical intermediates cause methane conversion to remain dominated by C 1 oxygenation rather than selective C─C coupling. Herein, we assemble the established Ni 3 (HITP) 2 framework (HITP = 2,3,6,7,10,11‐hexaiminotriphenylene) on PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene) to construct a molecular fence interface integrating Ni–N 4 sites with spatial confinement for selective C 2 coupling. During CEC, contact electrification at the PTFE–water interface supports radical generation for methane conversion, while the coupled Ni–N 4 sites further facilitate O 2 activation and modulate reactive species utilization. Simultaneously, the porous Ni 3 (HITP) 2 outer layer shows enhanced CH 4 uptake near the charged interface and is proposed to favor C─C coupling by promoting local methane enrichment and retention of methane‐derived intermediates. As a result, methane conversion is redirected from C 1 oxygenation toward selective C 2 coupling under ambient conditions, delivering a C 2 yield of 0.58 mmol g −1 h −1 with 82.4% selectivity. In situ spectroscopy and density functional theory calculations support a mechanistic model in which interfacial Ni–N 4 sites and the porous framework jointly influence reactive‐species utilization and methane‐derived intermediate reactions, favoring pathway‐selective methane CEC.

title: Biomimetic Molybdenum Chemistry Spanning all Four Molybdopterin Enzyme Families: From Stoichiometric Oxygen Atom Transfer to Catalytic C─H Oxidation
abstract: ABSTRACT Molybdopterin enzymes catalyze a diverse array of redox transformations, ranging from oxyanion reduction to C─H hydroxylation, through Mo VI /Mo IV cycling at active sites with conserved dithiolene‐coordinated structures. Synthetic models of these active sites have struggled to replicate this versatility in part due to comproportionation to inactive Mo V dimers, and catalytic turnover remains scarce. Here we report that a [N 2 S 2 ] 2− ‐supported Mo IV ═O complex abstracts oxygen atoms from substrates representative of three molybdopterin enzyme families: Me 2 SO, Me 3 NO, ClO 4 − , NO 3 − , and SeO 4 2− (DMSO reductases); methionine sulfoxide (sulfite oxidases); and benzamidoxime and N ‐hydroxyphthalimide (mARCs). In the cases of ClO 4 − and NO 3 − , oxygen atom transfer (OAT) requires Lewis acid activation by B(C 6 F 5 ) 3 . The corresponding Mo VI (O) 2 redox partner oxidizes formate via hydride abstraction, akin to formate dehydrogenases. The same complex has previously been shown to promote C─H hydroxylation of substrates inspired by the XO family, thus demonstrating reactivity that spans all four molybdopterin families. Coupling OAT and hydride transfer half‐reactions enables catalytic turnover, as demonstrated here for both benzimidazoline C─H hydroxylation and formate decarboxylation using DMSO as terminal oxidant, thus demonstrating the first examples of catalytic C─H oxidation by a molybdopterin‐inspired synthetic platform.

title: On‐Surface Non‐Equilibrium Phase Evolution Toward 2D Supramolecular Glass
abstract: ABSTRACT Controlling crystalline‐to‐glassy transitions represents a vibrant frontier in supramolecular chemistry and condensed matter physics, providing fundamental insights into non‐equilibrium dynamics and enabling functional tunability for elasticity electronics and phase‐change devices. Conventional two‐dimensional (2D) supramolecular assembly follows an enthalpy‐dominated thermodynamic paradigm, restricting the exploration of non‐equilibrium supramolecular glasses (SMGs). Herein, we report the controlled construction of a non‐equilibrium SMG on Ag(111) using in situ‐generated triradical triphenyl‐triazine molecules. The electrophilic triazine core enriches charge density at radical sites and strengthens molecule–substrate interfacial coupling, imposing pronounced kinetic constraints at the surface. Upon thermal activation, the system follows a non‐monotonic, four‐phase evolution that involves a thermodynamically uphill transformation. Rather than directly relaxing to the global thermodynamic minimum, it is kinetically arrested into a metastable glassy state with short‐range order and long‐range disorder. This work revises the conventional enthalpy‐dominated view of supramolecular assembly and establishes a backbone‐modulated radical kinetic strategy for rational fabrication of disorder‐tunable 2D supramolecular materials.

title: Interfacial Charge Modulation of Covalent Metal–Organic Frameworks for Efficient H 2 O 2 Electrosynthesis
abstract: ABSTRACT Electrochemical H 2 O 2 synthesis through the two‐electron oxygen reduction reaction offers a sustainable alternative to the energy‐intensive anthraquinone process. Crystalline porous frameworks are attractive for this route because of their structural precision, yet poor electrolyte wetting and limited electrochemical accessibility often restrict their practical performance. Here, we report an interfacial charge‐modulation strategy that transforms covalent metal–organic frameworks into highly wetted and electrochemically accessible catalytic interfaces. By incorporating cationic ethidium bromide units into a trinuclear copper‐pyrazolate framework, we construct EB‐Cu 3 ‐COF featuring enlarged interlayer spacing, enhanced interfacial charge transfer, and optimized *OOH intermediate adsorption. Consequently, EB‐Cu 3 ‐COF achieves up to 99% H 2 O 2 selectivity and a flow‐cell production rate of 39 420 mmol·g cat −1 ·h −1 , ranking among the best‐performing non‐pyrolyzed porous organic electrocatalysts reported to date. This work establishes interfacial charge‐modulation as a design principle for translating crystalline structural precision into electrochemically active interfaces.

title: Aluminum Scandium Nitride (AlScN) for Advanced Devices: Physical Mechanisms and Emerging Applications
abstract: ABSTRACT AlScN is an emerging semiconductor material that exhibits pronounced ferroelectric switching and enhanced piezoelectric responses through the incorporation of scandium (Sc) into aluminum nitride (AlN). These properties make AlScN a promising candidate for next‐generation ferroelectric in‐memory computing architecture and radio‐frequency circuits. However, challenges arise when preparing high‐quality epitaxial films with high Sc content, including insufficient ferroelectric endurance, interface instability, and leakage current, which collectively compromise device performance and reliability. This review provides a systematic overview of the ferroelectric and piezoelectric properties of AlScN with underlying physical mechanisms, highlights the challenges in material growth and device integration, and summarizes recent advances of emerging applications in piezoelectric devices, optoelectronic devices, ferroelectric memories, and high‐electron‐mobility transistors (HEMTs). Finally, perspectives are presented on future research directions, focusing on overcoming key barriers to device implementation. With ongoing advances in material optimization and system‐level integration, AlScN presents broad prospects for energy‐efficient computing and sensing hardware, accelerating the development of artificial intelligence (AI).

title: Polyzwitterion with Imidazole for Ultralow‐Power Organic Photoelectric Synaptic Transistors Achieving Multicolor Robot Vision and Dynamic Recognition
abstract: ABSTRACT Neuromorphic in‐sensor vision demands photoelectric synaptic transistors that co‐localize optical sensing and electrically tunable plasticity in a compact device, thereby simplifying artificial visual sensing circuits. Electrolytes and ionic liquids are widely employed as dielectric layers for neuromorphic transistors; however, cation–anion pairs without covalent bonds typically suffer from ion‐migration, ion replacement, and electrochemical reactions. These processes lead to current leakage, elevated power consumption, and irreversible drift, while photo‐modulation is further attenuated by exciton–polaron quenching. Here, to stabilize ionic charges and suppress ion‐migration, a polyzwitterion, poly(3‐(1‐vinyl‐3‐imidazolyl)‐propanesulfonate), is used as a single medium to unify electro‐ and photo‐synaptic functions, thereby simplifying the components and interfaces of the multilayer device. The aromatic conjugated imidazole ring stabilizes the cationic charge, and the covalently tethered cation–anion pair prevents long‐distance ion‐migration, ensuring strong cation–anion dipole polarization and reversible charge trapping. This enables robust multi‐wavelength photo‐synaptic modulation coupled with electro‐synaptic plasticity. The resulting organic photoelectric synaptic transistors achieve ultralow event energy consumption down to 10.95 aJ and support application‐relevant in‐sensor demonstrations, including encrypted image decoding, color‐guided robotic manipulation, pedestrian‐speed recognition, and motion prediction. These findings are poised to accelerate the development of multifunctional photoelectric synaptic devices and integrated sensing‐computing hardware architectures for artificial visual systems.

title: Engineered Excited‐State Coupling Enables Efficient Exciton Harvesting in Binuclear Copper Iodide Cluster Scintillators
abstract: ABSTRACT Environmentally benign scintillators with broadband radioluminescence are highly desirable for low‐cost, high‐performance x‐ray imaging. Recently, copper iodide (Cu–I) clusters have emerged as promising candidates, owing to strong spin‐orbit coupling, favorable solution processability, excellent x‐ray absorption efficiency, and efficient exciton harvesting enabled by aggregation‐induced emission and thermally activated delayed fluorescence. However, the mechanism by which aggregation‐state variation enhances the light yield by modulating intermolecular interactions remains poorly understood. Here, we establish a pair of isomeric Cu–I clusters with nearly identical x‐ray attenuation coefficients as a model platform to isolate and elucidate the role of intermolecular coupling. In this context, we uncover a breakthrough mechanistic picture in which engineered excited‐state coupling accelerates carrier relaxation and promotes efficient exciton harvesting and radiative recombination. Guided by this mechanism, water‐resistant cluster scintillator glasses with excellent processing flexibility are fabricated, delivering a high light yield of 32,456 photons MeV −1 and spatial resolution of 33.6 lp mm −1 . Furthermore, tandem integration with a high‐Z scintillator enables selective density‐discriminating x‐ray imaging and micro‐computed tomography. This work provides mechanistic guidance for ligand engineering in the design of efficient cluster scintillators and facilitates the high‐throughput development of promising metal‐cluster complexes for advanced optoelectronic applications.

title: Sequential Crystallization Decouples Cs 4 PbBr 6 and CsPbBr 3 Phases Enabling Efficient Perovskite Light‐Emitting Diodes
abstract: ABSTRACT Cesium lead bromide has emerged as a leading candidate for high‐performance perovskite light‐emitting diodes (PeLEDs) in next‐generation optoelectronics. However, the formation of the 0D Cs 4 PbBr 6 phase often accompanies CsPbBr 3 crystallization and is difficult to regulate, hampering the efficiency of LED devices in scalable production. In particular, 0D and 3D perovskite phases often crystallize as disordered structures, leading to poor crystalline quality and a high density of defects in the perovskite films. To address this challenge, we employed an additive‐mediated sequential crystallization (AMSC) strategy using 3‐carboxyphenylphosphonic acid (3‐CPPA) to modulate the crystallization kinetics of the 0D and 3D phases. Through strong interactions between the additive and perovskite precursors, the initial CsPbBr 3 formation is effectively slowed, allowing for temporally separated crystallization of Cs 4 PbBr 6 and CsPbBr 3 phases. This separated crystallization process significantly enhances the film quality of CsPbBr 3 phase. Remarkably, the AMSC strategy drives the Cs 4 PbBr 6 phase toward the film surface, thereby forming a favorable surface morphology and effectively improving the light outcoupling efficiency of PeLEDs. By leveraging this synergic strategy, we achieve an ultrahigh photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY) reaching nearly 100% and realize an efficient external quantum efficiency (EQE) of 35.3% in green PeLEDs, underscoring the critical role of phase crystallization engineering in optimizing perovskite emitters.

title: Electronic Coupling and Dual‐Spillover Effect in Co/Co 7 Fe 3 Heterointerface for Boosting Nitrate‐to‐Ammonia Conversion
abstract: ABSTRACT Rational design of dual‐site catalysts to decouple complex multi‐electron pathways is crucial for efficient electrocatalytic nitrate (NO 3 − ) reduction reaction (NO 3 RR). Here, we construct a Co/Co 7 Fe 3 heterojunction with strong electronic coupling that drives NO 3 RR efficiently via an unconventional [4+4] tandem mechanism. In this [4+4] pathway, the first 4‐electron step reduces NO 3 − to the *HNOH intermediate at the Fe sites. The second 4‐electron process involves the migration of *HNOH to adjacent Co sites, followed by a 4‐electron hydrogenation step. Experimental and theoretical investigations demonstrate that the interfacial electric field modulates the local water network, accelerating water dissociation and ensuring a robust proton supply via hydrogen spillover. Benefiting from well‐defined heterointerfaces, the adsorption energetics of key intermediates are favorably optimized, endowing Co/Co 7 Fe 3 with markedly boosted electrocatalytic activity for NO 3 RR through synergistic dual‐spillover effects, and enabling it to achieve a near‐unity Faradaic efficiency of 99.16% ± 0.3% and a remarkable NH 3 yield rate of 36.07 ± 0.52 mg h −1 cm −2 at −0.48 V versus RHE. Additionally, a rechargeable Zn‐nitrate battery featuring this material as the cathode delivers a peak power density of 18.15 mW cm −2 with excellent cycling stability. This study provides a novel paradigm for designing efficient tandem electrocatalysts.

title: Axial Cl‐Coordinated Porous FeCoZn Trimetallic Single‐Atom Catalysts: Breaking the Linear Scaling Relation for Superior Oxygen Reduction Reaction and Ultrastable Zinc‐Air Batteries
abstract: ABSTRACT Single‐atom catalysts (SACs) have emerged as a research frontier in electrocatalysis. However, conventional SACs possess single metal active sites, which hardly break the symmetry of geometric and electronic structure of M–N 4 . To address this limitation, porous trimetallic single‐atom catalysts (TACs) is fabricated via ZIF‐8‐derived ion exchange and gas‐phase etching methods. The catalyst features Fe, Co, and Zn single atoms with a special M–N 4 configuration where the three metal atoms share one N ligand. And axial coordination structure exists between Zn and Cl atoms. It exhibits outstanding oxygen reduction activity and stability under acidic/alkaline conditions, with a half‐wave potential of 0.81 V/0.96 V and loss of 4 mV/8 mV after 30 000 cycles. Only 6.5% performance decay is observed after 2163 h of charge‐discharge cycling in zinc‐air batteries (ZABs). Physicochemical characterization and density functional theory (DFT) calculations reveal that the trimetallic configuration breaks the geometric and electronic structural symmetry, optimizing the adsorption of intermediates during the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR). Axial coordination of Cl on Zn facilitates the bridge‐type adsorption of O 2 and breaks the linear scaling relationship. This work offers a novel strategy to break the symmetry of geometric and electronic structure of SACs and regulate reaction pathways.

title: Targeting Endoplasmic Reticulum Stress‐ROS‐Inflammation Cycle With Antibacterial Heterojunctions for Periodontitis Therapy
source: Wiley: Advanced Materials: Table of Contents
abstract: ABSTRACT In periodontitis, recalcitrant biofilms and the vicious endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress‐ROS‐inflammation cycle cause persistent inflammatory osteolysis. However, current treatments mainly alleviate infection and inflammation, without targeting this ER stress‐centered etiological circuit. Herein, we report the de novo design of an ER‐regulating heterojunction (ERR‐HJ), composed of cobalt selenide (CoSe), Ti 3 C 2 MXene, and taurine, for periodontitis treatment via bacterial clearance, ER homeostasis maintenance, and alveolar bone regeneration. Our studies demonstrate that the unique structure of the CoSe/Ti 3 C 2 heterojunction can scavenge ROS and easily transfer electrons from H 2 O 2 to bacterial membranes, which disrupts bacterial respiration and metabolism. At the cellular level, the heterojunction with taurine activates selenoprotein metabolism, restores redox balance, and alleviates ER stress by dampening the PERK‐CHOP pathway, collectively reprogramming macrophages towards a tissue‐regenerative M2 phenotype while inhibiting their osteoclastogenic differentiation. Strikingly, the osteogenic differentiation of human periodontal ligament cells is profoundly boosted. In periodontitis models, the ERR‐HJ promotes tissue repair and reduces alveolar bone resorption through concomitant suppression of oxidative stress, ER stress, and inflammation, suggesting the disruption of the self‐perpetuating cycle. This work furnishes an intriguing avenue for developing innovative heterojunction biomaterials to treat bacterial infection‐associated disorders by integrating bacterial killing and ER stress‐ROS‐inflammation cycle inhibition.

title: Morphological intelligence for dynamic aerial interactions
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Biological flyers achieve ecological dominance not through flight alone, but by seamlessly integrating aerial locomotion with forceful physical interactions, including snatching prey, perching on irregular surfaces, and operating across diverse media. Translating this agility into aerial robotics demands reconciling a fundamental conflict: impulsive, high-force actions destabilize the flight platform. Here, we present a bio-inspired unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) equipped with a mechanically intelligent impulsive limb that resolves this tradeoff through physical decoupling. An asymmetric bistable impulse module delivers a 2.3-fold extension within 70 ms, while a soft-linkage architecture reduces the transmission of impulsive interaction forces to the airframe. For the tested seven-segment configuration, intrinsic geometric tolerance corresponds to a passive vertical accommodation range of approximately 70% of the fully deployed arm length, reducing the need for precise altitude regulation within the tested range. We demonstrate the system’s multimodal capacity through dynamic in-flight snatching, energy-efficient perching, high-impact solid fracture, and cross-medium capture in viscous fluids, establishing a new paradigm for UAVs executing physically demanding tasks in complex environments.

title: Histone methyltransferase NSD2 shapes CD8+ T cell fates through the H3K36me2-Zbtb20 axis
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: CD8 + T cells, as the most important cytolytic cells in adaptive immunity, can differentiate into distinct subpopulations with specific functions and fates. During this process, CD8 + T cells exhibit substantial plasticity in their differentiation trajectory. Notably, epigenetic regulation has emerged as a pivotal mechanism to govern T cell fate decisions. In this study, we demonstrate that the histone methyltransferase NSD2 critically regulates CD8 + T cell differentiation during acute viral infection. While NSD2 deficiency enhances the early expansion of activated CD8 + T cells, it severely compromises their survival fitness during the contraction phase, leading to a disproportionate collapse of the antigen-specific pool and limiting the establishment of robust long-lived memory. Mechanistically, this defect is driven by the disruption of the H3K36me2- Zbtb20 regulatory axis. Furthermore, we show that in the absence of NSD2, CD8 + T cells in tumor exhibit an increased proportion but dysfunctional resident memory T cell phenotype. Collectively, our findings highlight a critical role for NSD2 in providing more mechanistic insights into how epigenetic mechanisms fine-tune T cell differentiation.

title: SCML2 inhibits PrimPol-mediated DNA replication repriming and regulates replication gap-associated cancer cell vulnerability
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: PrimPol-mediated fork repriming generates single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) gaps during DNA damage tolerance (DDT), which, if not properly repaired, can threaten genomic stability. PrimPol is a highly error-prone polymerase. Thus, PrimPol activity should be tightly regulated to fit into DDT and remain low during unstressed DNA replication. Human sex comb on midleg like-2 (SCML2), a Polycomb protein containing MBT repeats, has been identified as a component of the noncanonical PRC1 complex and a regulator of p53 and CHK1 stability. Here, we show that SCML2A is a suppressor of PrimPol. SCML2A directly binds two domains of PrimPol: Its RBR domain binds the C terminus of PrimPol, and its SAM domain binds the amino-terminal AEP domain, thereby inhibiting ssDNA-binding capacity of the AEP domain. SCML2 depletion leads to increased nascent DNA synthesis and accumulation of PrimPol-mediated ssDNA gaps under replication stress. SCML2 depletion also enhances PrimPol engagement during unstressed DNA replication, leading to subsequent accumulation of ssDNA gaps, which are filled by REV1/POLζ-mediated translesion synthesis (TLS) and RAD51-mediated template switching (TS). SCML2 depletion confers cellular hypersensitivity to RAD51 or REV1/POLζ inhibition, which is associated with increased accumulation of ssDNA gaps. Furthermore, CDK2 phosphorylates SCML2A at Ser 267 , which suppresses RBR-mediated PrimPol interaction. Cyclin E1 overexpression leads to CDK2-mediated SCML2A Ser 267 hyperphosphorylation, which releases the inhibitory effect of SCML2A on PrimPol and subsequently induces ssDNA gap accumulation. Collectively, we identify SCML2A as a negative regulator of PrimPol.

title: Interferon-λ signaling to maternal dendritic cells protects against congenital Zika virus infection
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Interferon-λ (IFN-λ, type III IFN) mediates antiviral immunity at anatomic barriers, including the maternal-fetal interface. To investigate the effects of IFN-λ during congenital Zika virus (ZIKV) infection, we infected mice lacking the IFN-αβ receptor ( Ifnar1 −/− ) or both the IFN-αβ and IFN-λ receptors ( Ifnar1 −/− Ifnlr1 −/− ) at embryonic day 9 and found that loss of maternal IFN-λ signaling resulted in greater transplacental transmission, highlighting a protective effect of IFN-λ at the maternal-fetal interface. To investigate the spatial relationship between ZIKV infection and antiviral responses, we used HiPlex RNAscope on the entire gravid uterus and found that IFN-λ was expressed more proximal to the site of ZIKV infection in Ifnar1 −/− dams compared to Ifnar1 −/− Ifnlr1 −/− dams. We performed immunophenotyping of the placenta and uterus by flow cytometry and found a decrease in dendritic cells and natural killer (NK) cells in the uterus of Ifnar1 −/− Ifnlr1 −/− dams compared to Ifnar1 −/− dams, but NK cell depletion did not affect fetal infection. Using conditional knockout mice, we identified maternal dendritic cells as the key IFN-λ–responsive cell type mediating protection against ZIKV congenital infection. Together, our data support a model in which IFN-λ signaling to maternal dendritic cells increases dendritic cell accumulation in the uterus, which facilitates a protective antiviral response that restricts ZIKV congenital infection.

title: CASTOR1 functional inactivation drives KRAS-mutant NSCLC and therapy resistance by a noncanonical mechanism of tumor suppression
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: CASTOR1, a cytosolic arginine sensor and regulator of mTORC1 signaling, is identified here as a tumor suppressor in KRAS -driven non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). In a KRAS G12D mouse model, CASTOR1 deletion enhances tumor initiation and progression, accompanied by increased proliferation. Although CASTOR1 is rarely mutated or deleted in human cancers, its expression progressively declines during tumor progression and is associated with increased AKT activation and CASTOR1 phosphorylation, consistent with functional inactivation. Loss of CASTOR1 results in constitutive mTORC1 hyperactivation, impaired arginine-dependent regulation of mTORC1 signaling, elevated p-4EBP1 and p-S6 levels, increased AKT and ERK activation, genomic instability, and resistance to KRAS G12D inhibitors. Tumors and tumor-derived organoids deficient in CASTOR1 are resistant to KRAS inhibition, but this resistance can be overcome by cotargeting mTORC1 or dual PI3K/mTOR inhibition. These findings identify CASTOR1 as a critical link between nutrient sensing and oncogenic signaling and reveal its functional inactivation as an important mechanism contributing to KRAS -driven NSCLC progression and therapeutic resistance. The results further support rational combination therapies to overcome KRAS inhibitor resistance in CASTOR1-low NSCLC.

title: Death receptors regulate entry to therapy-induced senescence and orchestrate addiction to IAPs
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Cytotoxic chemotherapy typically results in the elimination of a fraction of the tumor with surviving cells entering a state of persistence or premature replicative senescence that can lead to recurrence. Here, we show that therapy-induced senescence is associated with robust up-regulation of Fas and/or TRAIL-R2/DR5 death receptors in vitro and in vivo. The latter receptors restricted entry to senescence and exerted selective pressure on senescent cells through promoting assembly of proapoptotic receptor-interacting protein kinase 1 (RIPK1)/Fas-associated death domain protein (FADD)/Caspase-8 “FADDosome” complexes, restrained by cFLIP L . Accordingly, deletion of CASP-8 robustly enhanced entry to senescence and prolonged the life span of senescent cells. cIAP-2, which inhibits death receptor–driven cell death, was also up-regulated in senescent cells, and deletion of IAPs suppressed entry to senescence. Consistent with this, small-molecule IAP antagonists exhibited potent senolytic activity through enhancing death receptor–initiated Caspase-8 activation. Thus, death receptor–driven assembly of RIPK1/FADD/Caspase-8 complexes in senescent cells orchestrates addiction to IAPs that can be exploited by IAP antagonists.

title: Electrically reconfigurable dipolar polaritons with highly tunable nonlinearity in a homobilayer microcavity
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Active control over optical nonlinearity in solid-state systems is central to unlocking exotic many-body phenomena and photonic devices. While exciton-polaritons in transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) offer a promising platform, their practical utility is impeded by fixed interactions and a trade-off between nonlinearity and oscillator strength. Here, we report electrically tunable dipolar polaritons in a dual-gated bilayer MoS 2 microcavity, demonstrating in situ reshaping of the dispersion and modulation of the light-matter coupling strength via the quantum-confined Stark effect. Crucially, this electrical control yields a seven-fold enhancement of the polariton-polariton interaction strength. This enhancement arises from the combined tuning of the effective exciton-exciton interaction and the excitonic Hopfield coefficient. In addition, electrostatic doping provides an independent knob to continuously drive a strong-to-weak coupling crossover. Our findings establish dual-gated TMD homobilayer as a versatile platform for on-chip, dynamically reconfigurable nonlinear light-matter physics.

title: In situ CAR-M engineered by liposomal mRNA nanomedicine remodels fibrotic microenvironment for ameliorating liver fibrosis
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Liver fibrosis is a severe complication of diverse chronic liver diseases characterized by a dysregulated hepatic microenvironment, and effective clinical therapeutic strategies for this condition remain lacking to date. Chimeric antigen receptor macrophages (CAR-Ms) hold considerable therapeutic potential for liver fibrosis via antigen-specific recognition and efferocytotic activity, yet their clinical translation is largely hindered by the sophisticated ex vivo preparation procedures. Herein, we report an in situ CAR-M engineering strategy that uses a phosphatidylserine (PS)–incorporated, macrophage-targeted lipid nanoparticle (LNP) for the codelivery of CAR messenger RNA (mRNA) and Cas9 mRNA in vivo. Our findings demonstrate that this engineered LNP achieves efficient targeting of liver-resident macrophages. Transfection with fibroblast activation protein α (FAPα)–CAR mRNA equips macrophages with the capacity to specifically target activated hepatic stellate cells (aHSCs), whereas Cas9-mediated follistatin-like protein 1 (FSTL-1) gene editing enhances the efferocytotic function of macrophages in liver tissues. Consequently, functional CAR-Ms are generated in situ, which elicits robust antifibrotic effects, including reduced collagen deposition, restored sinusoidal architecture and enhanced immune-mediated antifibrotic activity. Collectively, our customized LNP-mediated in situ engineering of liver macrophages into CAR-Ms enables precise antifibrotic intervention for liver fibrosis and circumvents the cumbersome ex vivo CAR-M preparation process.

title: Neural circuitry mediating hypercapnia-induced microarousal and impaired sleep depth
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Sleep disruption in obstructive sleep apnea syndrome is characterized by frequent microarousals and reduced sleep depth, yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we show that intermittent hypercapnic air (HA) induces time-locked microarousals, fragments sleep, reduces non–rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep depth, and diminishes rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. HA exposure activates glutamatergic neurons in the nucleus tract solitary (NTS Vglut2 ), and their optogenetic or chemogenetic activation is sufficient to trigger arousal and impair sleep. Projection-specific activation reveals that NTS Vglut2 projections to the paraventricular nucleus (PVN), parabrachial nucleus (PB), paraventricular thalamus, and locus coeruleus (LC) promote arousal, whereas projections to the PB and LC additionally reduce NREM sleep depth. Inhibition of NTS Vglut2 projection to the PVN significantly postpones HA-induced arousal. NTS Vglut2 terminals monosynaptically activate corticotropin-releasing hormone neurons in the PVN (PVN CRH ), and inhibition of PVN CRH neurons or knockdown of Slc17a6 (encoding Vglut2), but not Crh , delays hypercapnia-induced arousal. These findings identify neural circuits underlying hypercapnia-induced microarousal and reduced sleep depth.

title: RAF isoform selectivity of MEK inhibitors and rational design of a covalent ARAF-MEK inhibitor
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Aberrant activation of the RAS/RAF/mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase (MEK)/extracellular signal–regulated kinase pathway is a frequent cause of cancer. Allosteric MEK inhibitors block this pathway by binding RAF-MEK complexes to prevent activation of MEK by RAF. However, how MEK inhibitor potency varies across the three RAF isoforms remains poorly understood. We profiled seven allosteric MEK inhibitors and observed a notable hierarchy of sensitivity: All most potently inhibited CRAF-driven MEK activation while relatively sparing ARAF-driven activation. We identified point mutations in ARAF and CRAF proximate to the MEK inhibitor binding site that markedly altered inhibitor sensitivity. Using a rational design approach, we developed a more potent inhibitor of ARAF-driven MEK signaling, TWG-07-148. Our cryo–electron microscopy structure shows how this acrylamide-containing analog of MEK inhibitor trametinib covalently targets Cys 514 , a residue unique to ARAF. Our studies highlight the importance of the activating RAF isoform as a determinant of MEK inhibitor sensitivity and provide proof of concept for the development of MEK inhibitors that more effectively block ARAF-driven MEK signaling via covalent targeting of Cys 514 .

title: Biophysically constrained learning from healthy neural priors improves motor decoding in pathological cortical networks
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: High-performance brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) rely on stable neural representations, yet brain functional impairments inherently disrupt canonical encoding, creating a fundamental decoding paradox. Conventional data-driven approaches struggle to bridge this gap because of pathological data scarcity and heterogeneity. Here, we propose to leverage healthy neural priors and introduce Pathology-Aware Consensus Training (PACT), a paradigm embedding biophysical constraints into healthy neural recordings to guide neural decoding. In a gesture classification task using high-density electrocorticography from patients with gliomas infiltrating the motor cortex, PACT improved the accuracy by more than 10%, effectively restoring the distorted semantic geometry of motor commands and realigning them with healthy canonical representations (correlation increase: r = 0.66 to r = 0.94). Mechanistically, PACT induced an emergent “inverse weighting” strategy: The model autonomously suppresses high-power pathological noise while reanchoring spatial attention to functional compensatory regions. This study provides a proof of concept for improving decoding in compromised networks by harnessing healthy neural dynamics, laying the theoretical foundation for future BCI deployments in clinical populations.

title: Using initial states to identify successful El Niño–Southern Oscillation forecasts 1 year in advance
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) is the primary source of climate predictability on seasonal and longer timescales over much of the globe, but predicting its phase beyond 9 months has remained challenging. Here, we leverage an underappreciated factor in ENSO forecasting: the substantial variation in forecast skill based on the ENSO phase at the time a forecast is issued. Our analysis of transitions between ENSO phases in a dynamical hindcast dataset demonstrates that this variation markedly exceeds intermodel differences in predictive capability. Forecasts initialized during La Niña conditions perform best, with three models correctly predicting transitions to El Niño 1 year in advance over 70% of the time. We present our findings in a simple framework that allows decision-makers to assess the likelihood of a forecast being correct on the basis of the current ENSO state. Applied effectively, these findings could improve long-lead ENSO forecasting strategies, enhancing global risk management.

title: Frequency-dependent fitness effects are ubiquitous in rapidly adapting microbial populations
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: In simple microbial populations, the fitness effects of selected mutations are typically assumed to be constant, regardless of mutant frequency. This assumption underpins predictions about evolutionary dynamics, epistasis, and the maintenance of genetic diversity. Here, we systematically test this assumption using beneficial mutations from early generations of the Escherichia coli long-term evolution experiment (LTEE). Using flow cytometry–based competition assays, we find that frequency-dependent fitness effects are the norm rather than the exception, occurring in ∼80% of strain pairs tested. Most competitions exhibit negative frequency dependence, where fitness advantages decline as mutant frequency increases. We demonstrate that the strength of frequency dependence is predictable from invasion fitness measurements, which explain approximately half of the biological variation in frequency-dependent slopes. We also observe violations of fitness transitivity in several strain combinations, indicating that competitive outcomes cannot always be predicted from fitness measured against a single reference strain. High-resolution measurements reveal that frequency dependence changes substantially within the growth cycle, with the net per-cycle effect reflecting the balance of opposing dynamics at different growth phases. Our results demonstrate that, even in a model system designed to minimize ecological complexity, subtle interactions between closely related genotypes create frequency-dependent selection that can fundamentally alter evolutionary trajectories.

title: A methylation-dependent reader couples arginine methylation to S6K2 signaling in vivo
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Arginine methylation regulates diverse cellular processes, yet how methyl-arginine reader proteins couple this modification to kinase signaling in vivo remains poorly defined. Here, we identify staphylococcal nuclease and Tudor domain containing 1 (SND1) as a pancreas-enriched effector that links symmetric dimethylarginine (SDMA) recognition to S6 kinase 2 (S6K2) activation. Disruption of SDMA-mediated binding by a point mutation in the SND1 Tudor domain markedly diminishes ribosomal protein S6 (S6) phosphorylation in the pancreas. Mechanistically, SND1 engages SDMA-modified arginines within the carboxyl-terminal glycine-arginine–rich (GAR) motif of S6K2 and promotes S6K2-dependent S6 phosphorylation. Mice harboring lysine substitutions at these GAR arginines ( S6k2 RK) phenocopy Snd1 Tudor-mutant ( Snd1 knock-in) animals, exhibiting impaired pancreatic S6 phosphorylation. Transcriptomic analyses reveal extensive overlap in dysregulated pathways between Snd1 and S6k2 mutant pancreata, supporting a shared signaling cascade. Together, these findings establish a methylation-dependent reader-kinase axis that links protein arginine methyltransferase 5–catalyzed arginine methylation to tissue-specific control of ribosome signaling and cellular stress adaptation.

title: Structural basis for start codon selection by eIF5-mimic proteins
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Start codon selection extensively regulates the cellular proteome and is implicated in cancer and other diseases. The eIF5-mimic proteins (5MPs: 5MP1/BZW2 and 5MP2/BZW2) restrict non-AUG start codon usage and thereby reprogram proteoform expression from mRNAs with alternative start sites, such as the oncogenic c-Myc. Here, using in extracto cryo–electron microscopy (cryo-EM) and biochemical assays, we report how 5MP represses translation dependent on the sequence context at start codons. Cryo-EM structures of 48 S preinitiation complexes (PICs) reveal 5MP1 bound at the A site of the small ribosomal subunit. 5MPs act as initiation factors that stabilize an open PIC conformation, promoting mRNA scanning and inhibiting initiation at suboptimal start codons. We propose to designate 5MP as eIF1S (eukaryotic initiation factor 1 scanning). These findings reveal the structural basis for proteome modulation by 5MPs and may help correct dysregulated translation in disease.

title: Scalable architecture for measurement-induced squeezed light interferometers
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Scalable interferometers lie at the heart of photonic quantum technologies, but their expansion has been fundamentally limited by optical losses that grow with circuit depth. Here, we introduce and experimentally demonstrate a measurement-induced architecture for multimode squeezed-light interferometers that overcomes this barrier. By shifting complexity from deep optical networks to programmable homodyne measurements, we realize effective transformations within a shallow, low-loss platform. We validate the principle with a six-mode device and extend it to a 400-mode interferometer, marking a leap in scale beyond conventional designs. Crucially, this strategy not only enables scalable squeezed light interferometry but also provides a powerful route to the generation of large-scale entangled states—a key requirement for quantum computing, simulation, and communication. Our results establish measurement-induced circuits as a practical pathway toward noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) applications and future demonstrations of quantum advantage.

title: Polycomb factor PHF19 affects AML initiation, patient prognosis, and survival
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is marked by unchecked expansion of undifferentiated myeloid cells. Although oncogenic fusions such as MLL-AF9 can initiate disease, the early steps of leukemogenesis and the role of cell-intrinsic regulators remain unclear. We previously showed that the Polycomb-associated factor Phf19 is required for hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) maintenance and state control in mice and that its loss (Phf19 KO ) impairs HSC function. To define Phf19’s role in transformation, we expressed MLL-AF9 in Phf19 KO hematopoietic cells and performed integrated multiomic analyses. Phf19 deletion promoted acquisition of stemlike features and reduced responsiveness to differentiation-inducing AML therapies. Molecular and functional consequences of Phf19 loss paralleled those observed in the datasets of patients with AML. From these data, we derived a prognostic signature—PHFScore—which reveals previously unrecognized AML survival-correlating genes that robustly stratify patients across distinct cellular origins and leukemogenic stages, underscoring Phf19’s key role in AML biology and prognosis.

title: Spider-inspired bidirectional robotic joints driven by electrohydraulic multiaxial strain
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Compared with conventional motors and servos, soft-actuated angular-motion devices are superior in environmental adaptability and human-robot interaction, yet they can only achieve active bidirectional angular motion by integrating antagonistic actuators or restriction modules. The integration of such components introduces deformation antagonism, compromises structural simplicity, and increases control complexity. Herein, we propose a spider-inspired centimeter-scale soft bidirectional robotic joint driven by a pair of synchronously controlled electrohydraulic actuators (EHAs). Specifically, the EHAs generate multiaxial strain, enabling the joint to bidirectionally rotate depending on its physical state, without introducing additional functional components or asynchronous controllers. Furthermore, the joint demonstrates (i) high-speed (forward: 2851° per second, reverse: 1934° per second) and wide-stroke (up to 156.8°) rotational performance, (ii) multimodal motion (e.g., self-unfolding, self-folding, and reciprocating swinging), (iii) continuous response (up to 40 hertz), and (iv) payload-bearing capability. Last, three joint-integrated devices validate its feasibility as a multifunctional, high-dynamic, and single-channel-controlled actuation component in diverse robotic applications. This work establishes a viable design framework for minimalist yet versatile bioinspired robots.

title: Bioinspired ventral-groove fibers for volume-programmable pneumatic actuation
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Pneumatic actuation plays a central role in soft robotics, with conventional systems relying on pressure-driven chamber deformation and closed-loop feedback for precise control. Here, we introduce bioinspired ventral-groove filamentary fibers that reframe pneumatic actuation from pressure-dominated chambers to volume-programmable fiber architectures, enabling previously unexplored robotic capabilities. Coupling microgroove unfolding with elastic expansion, these molecularly programmed fibers achieve reversible 400× area expansion at ultralow pressure (∼0.8 kPa) and scale from ∼100 μm to centimeter-scale diameters and tens of meters in length, supporting micro- to macro-scale robotic systems. We demonstrate responsive textile actuation through an everyday flotation garment with 20-m fibers seamlessly integrated into clothing. We also show a gripping approach with three capabilities: disturbance-robust high-precision grasping, conformal handling of fragile nerve-like filaments and delicate incense-ash cones, and open-loop operation that reduces reliance on sensory feedback. By establishing a volume-programmable actuation paradigm, this work paves the way for low-pressure pneumatic technologies in soft robotics and responsive textiles.

title: Multiplexed and implantable fiber sensor for real-time blood monitoring
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Accurate and real-time monitoring of blood electrolyte composition, particularly sodium (Na + ) and potassium (K + ), is crucial for guiding intraoperative and postoperative decisions, as these ions regulate critical bodily functions such as cardiac rhythm and fluid balance. Current blood analysis relies on ex vivo blood sampling, which introduces substantial time delays and can be susceptible to inaccuracies caused by temperature fluctuations. To address these challenges, we report here a multiplexed and implantable fiber sensor (MIFS) capable of monitoring Na + and K + ions in real time directly in the bloodstream. MIFS integrates three parallel liquid metal channels with a multilayer surface-electrode architecture, which synergistically enhances sensitivity, minimizes sensing drift, ensures mechanical flexibility, and offers outstanding biocompatibility for vascular implantation. In vivo testing in rabbit models and validation in human blood samples demonstrate MIFS’s superior sensing accuracy, real-time, and stable sensing in agreement with conventional ex vivo measurements. This work paves the way for real-time blood monitoring in clinical practice.

title: Capillary physics links HIV capsid geometry to nuclear pore translocation
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: The protective capsid encasing the genetic material of HIV can traverse the nuclear pore complex (NPC) intact, despite being far larger than conventional passive cargo. This is attributed to the properties of the capsid surface, which promote partitioning into cohesive assemblies of the disordered proteins that form the NPC’s permeability barrier: phenylalanine-glycine nucleoporins (FG-Nups). The implication, at the mesoscale, is that capsid–NPC interactions are characterized by the interfacial physics of wetting and capillarity. To capture this, we develop a minimal theory that reduces to an interplay between capsid geometry, effective cytoplasmic and nucleoplasmic contact angles, and a ratio of interfacial tensions. By combining analytical calculations, sharp- and diffuse-interface numerics, we make several predictions: A geometry-dependent trade-off between penetration depth and the wetting transition; asymmetric capillary forces that generate torques and lead to metastable “stalled” states that are tilted; a topological classification of the possible mechanisms underlying the largest energetic barrier; and spontaneous symmetry breaking of displaced FG-Nups. These behaviors connect capsid shape and orientation to the topology and symmetry of FG-Nup displacement, and to the molecular compositions on each side of the pore. They are consistent with published cryoelectron tomography orientations, which provide an initial estimate of the cytoplasmic contact angle. Crucially, our results identify a capillary advantage for the HIV capsid’s characteristic broken-symmetry geometry.

title: Action features dominate cortical representation during natural vision
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Cortical resources are allocated into systems specialized for processing ecologically relevant features of the world. These features are typically studied in isolation using controlled experimental stimuli, making it difficult to assess the relative importance of different kinds of features that tend to overlap during natural vision. In the current study, we evaluated the relative contributions of action, agent, and scene features in predicting cortical activity while participants viewed a 1-h nature documentary. We tested four sets of model features: semantic vectors capturing the observed action, agent, and scene features derived from an annotation of the stimulus, as well as low-level visual motion-energy features. We used banded ridge regression to fit vertex-wise encoding models from the combination of all four sets of features. While each set of features predicted neural activity in the expected areas, the action features predicted more widespread activity. A variance partitioning analysis revealed that the action features captured the most unique variance in neural activity across a much larger extent of cortex than the agent or scene features. Our findings suggest that cortical activity during dynamic, natural vision is dominated by features for understanding the actions of others.

title: NRF2 coordinates cystine import and glutathione use to sustain ferroptosis resistance and formaldehyde tolerance in cancer
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Cancer cells must balance detoxification of reactive metabolic by-products while preserving redox homeostasis, but how this trade-off is managed remains unclear. The Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (KEAP1)–nuclear factor–erythroid 2–related factor 2 (NRF2) pathway, a key regulator of antioxidant defenses, is frequently hyperactivated in cancer. Formaldehyde, a genotoxic one-carbon by-product, is typically detoxified via glutathione (GSH), which is also essential for suppressing ferroptotic cell death. Here, we show that NRF2 promotes formaldehyde tolerance through up-regulation of the cystine transporter SLC7A11, enabling a protective mechanism that is largely independent of GSH, which remains necessary for ferroptosis resistance. In NRF2-active cells, formaldehyde reacts with cysteine to form a thiazolidine conjugate, and the combination of formaldehyde stress and SLC7A11 inhibition activates the integrated stress response, suppresses global protein synthesis, and markedly compromises cell viability. Together, these findings reveal that NRF2 coordinates ferroptosis resistance and formaldehyde tolerance, exposing a cancer vulnerability through combined inhibition of cystine uptake and GSH synthesis.

title: Education reduces dementia incidence and mitigates genetic risk
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: There is little causal evidence on factors that can protect individuals against Alzheimer’s Disease and Related Dementias (ADRD) risk. We study the causal effect of education on ADRD, exploiting a regression discontinuity generated by a compulsory schooling reform. ADRD was ascertained based on medical history, hospital records, and death registries, addressing concerns about selective sample attrition. We find that education reduces incidence of ADRD. Using molecular genetic data, we show that the reform weakened the relationship between genetics and ADRD incidence, implying genetic risk of dementia is not immutable and can be modified by social policy.

title: Si-scRNA-seq: Enabling ambient-stable single-cell transcriptomics through spatially confined biosilicification
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) is constrained by rapid RNA degradation during sample storage, necessitating cold-chain logistics. Here we present spatially confined biosilicification (SCB), wherein RNA is encapsulated within a nanoscopic layer of amorphous silicon dioxide, as a highly effective methodology enabling ambient-temperature preservation of single-cell transcriptomes. By judiciously incorporating a silicification inhibitor, SCB achieves spatiotemporal control over both intra- and extracellular silica deposition, preventing excessive crosslinking and cell aggregation while preserving RNA biointegrity and accessibility. scRNA-seq performed with biosilicified cells (Si-scRNA-seq) maintained high transcriptomic fidelity with fresh samples (R
                    2
                    = 0.95 after 7 d) extending RNA half-life to 54.8 d at 25 °C, a 685-fold improvement compared to unprotected samples. Furthermore, Si-scRNA-seq confers robust resistance against oxidative and UV degradation. Compatible with mainstream platforms at ~0.1 RMB per sample, Si-scRNA-seq successfully resolves cellular heterogeneity in clinical lung, liver, and ovarian cancer specimens after extended room-temperature storage. Si-scRNA-seq provides a scalable and cold-chain–free solution for single-cell transcriptomics in research and clinical settings.
